en: Preface to the Commentary on the Heart Sutra:
Master Zhuang Chanliang Xuhui has cultivated his practice for thirty years; his ears hear no extraneous sounds and his mouth utters no idle words.

He takes his meals like a wandering cloud or drifting water, and those who arrive find in him a homecoming. Ziyeyuan, Huaisun, and Xiyan were likewise men of refined austerity who stood out from the crowd.
A scholar from the Wu region, possessing a wild and unconventional spirit, passed away early in life after entrusting the affairs of the monastery to Master Yuan.

He would sit in meditation in a single room, performing the six periods of worship to the Buddha without ceasing through cold or heat. Later, he visited Sanfeng, where they found great joy in their mutual affinity.

Among Sanfeng’s disciples who had attained the Dharma—such as [Name] and others—all regarded him with the respect due to an elder; none dared to treat him with arrogance on account of what they did not know.
He lived in solitude according to worldly custom, and none could fathom his limits; this is all I know of him. We never met through written texts.

During the winter and spring, we would occasionally pass each other, and whenever there was a rustling sound from within his sleeves, he would produce a volume—a commentary on the Heart Sūtra—which he would show me. At this, I was utterly bewildered.
Furthermore, I did not dare to bestow praise upon these writings at random, as others might do, thereby increasing my verbal karma;

rather, I urged that they be brought quickly to completion and corrected according to what are called the Great Dharma Masters of today—such as Master Zhongfeng of Mount Hua and Master Chongguang—and all of them nodded their approval.
Consequently, I devised a plan to have them carved into printing blocks as a means of ensuring their immortality, for this was a necessity born of my own feelings regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Those who grasp it through the mere joining of brushstrokes and ink are superficial; those who comprehend it with their minds are profound.
You, sir, have sat and reclined in deep contemplation, reciting and savoring these words morning and night, doing nothing but this.

Since you are thus able to accord upward with the intent of the Buddha and not err downward against the commentators, this single volume is sufficient; there is no need to seek more. The world is desolate, and the worthy man remains hidden.

I humbly beseech you, sir, merely to clarify and purify your mind and spirit while maintaining your vow; in a future life, you will surely become a great master to expound upon Prajñā and awaken the deluded masses.

Now that your years are advanced and your remaining radiance is not long, you should like a skilled merchant who keeps his treasures deep within and seeks neither fame nor success. This is my high hope for you, sir.
On the twenty-third day of the eighth month of the fourteenth year of the Chongzhen era, the disciple Xu Bo wrote this preface for the *Prajñā Jìjué* (Decisions on the Boundary of Prajñā).
I have often heard that when one person attains the Way, they naturally possess a unique method for proclaiming and spreading it; it is like a lamp, whose light originates from its flame.
Being able to illuminate the principles of phenomena for oneself, one cannot help but do so; therefore, after the Bodhisattva Mingxing attained awakening, the Golden Mouth (the Buddha) praised him.
This praise was for his wisdom and virtuous marks, which enable all beings to hear and know them—not something produced out of resentment or pent-up emotion.
As for those who know this, there are levels of depth; in its proclamation, there is inevitably the sudden and the gradual. How could it be that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas merely...

Ceasing the practice of the *tathāgatagarbha* as a provisional city, the bodhisattva’s conduct proceeds deeply and directly toward the precious abode. This [teaching] belongs to other sections and is not the primary exposition here;

rather, this is the Middle Way of neither existence nor non-existence. Having discarded the conditions of the nine realms and exhausted the sentiments of both sages and ordinary beings, one acts solely through this.
Although there may be attachments and inversions, none are not entirely abandoned; thus the fruits of both Bodhi and Nirvana are simultaneously realized. Thus it is said in the Sūtra: [text follows].
The King opened this [text], which is entirely the pearl from the topknot with nothing else besides; the Elder of Beichan, Master Liangxuhui, for thirty years has focused solely on this.
Suddenly, he let it slip, borrowing the old to expound the new and proclaiming this primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).

This is not like those who merely parrot words without having attained anything. Recently, as the work was being prepared for the printing blocks, I respectfully inscribed these remarks upon its cover.
Written by the retired monk Zhengxing of Tōgikei on the day before the Mid-Autumn Festival in the year of Xinsi during the Chongzhen era,
at the Bānruò Jìjué chamber within the Tianlong annex to the east of the Jingfan Altar.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Xuanzang, by Imperial Edict.
Expounded by the Śramaṇa Dahui of Beichen Monastery in Wumen, Ming Dynasty.
The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra)
Prajñā is wisdom. This wisdom appears within the inconceivable; its gathering and dispersing never depart from a single atom. Why is this?
Because this prajñā is the designation of the fundamental limit (*koṭi*). Thus, when the World-Honored One beheld the morning star, he exclaimed:
"How marvelous! All sentient beings are endowed with the wisdom and virtues of the Tathāgata."

How could these marks be seen in a single kṣaṇa? Beyond the sight of the stars, there further exist body and mind, ordinary beings and sages, pure and impure lands, and all sentient beings who realize them together;
this is what is called "possessing" [the marks]. As for *pāramitā*, it means "reaching the other shore";
reaching the other shore of the primordial limit (*koṭi*) is its meaning. This primordial limit is the very self of all sentient beings.
Abiding in one's original dwelling, one does not attain it through cultivation; yet people today falsely claim there is a "far shore" to be reached, laboring in vain until the end of kalpas.
Yet Nirvana has, from the beginning, never moved even an inch. One can see that what is truly appropriate is to return directly to the source without seeking truth elsewhere.
Otherwise, there will inevitably be the failure to dissolve the opposition of self and other, leading to the arising of birth and death.
To die here is to lose the essential purport of this sutra. This *prajñā-citta* (wisdom-mind) is that which both sages and ordinary beings alike receive and are endowed with by common lot.
Because ordinary beings cling to deluded thoughts, there arise various distinctions; because the worthy and the sagely cling to their practices, there likewise arise various distinctions.
However, if one discusses the fundamental dharma within the mind and conduct of ordinary beings and sages, [there is no such differentiation].
Ultimately, all are established within the span of a single kṣaṇa; therefore, the Sūtra says:
"All worthies and sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). "Sūtra" means permanence; it signifies the sense of thorough penetration.
Every word and phrase of this single Sūtra—whether spoken or silent, whether moving or still—is expounded throughout every atom and every moment.
The Dharma of the true, eternal, and swift path ultimately converges within a single moment (*kṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*), wherein a single path runs through it all.
According to this, when the World-Honored One entered the *kṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*, he did not depart from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
even throughout the seven locations and nine assemblies, he likewise never left the site of enlightenment. This is precisely "no-time. It is no-time.
This does not pass even for a moment and does not omit the three periods of time; it responds to conditions and meets with stimuli without losing its fundamental limit.
Therefore, regarding Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:

"Avalokita" (The Observer) refers to the function of wisdom, and "Īśvara" (The Sovereign) refers to the unconditioned nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Thus, one contemplates by means of the correspondence between subject and object.

Thus, non-sovereignty must involve the simultaneous forgetting of both subject and object; only when they are blended and integrated without distinction does one become a sovereign Bodhisattva—a "Bodhisattva" being one who has awakened to sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is said that the Wisdom Body of Universal Salvation pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
this Universal Salvation of sentient beings, wherein both the savior and the saved are ultimately subsumed within the Wisdom Body, is precisely what is meant by the Dharma Body.
"When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*":

the phrase "practicing the profound *prajñā*" and so forth implies that *prajñā* is common to both ordinary beings and sages; regardless of whether it concerns the primary retribution of the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) with its marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), or the secondary retribution of the lands of atoms adorned with various jewels, or the sentient beings and their environments—both primary and secondary—all ultimately return [to this].
To reach the ultimate limit—the Dharma-body, the eternally quiescent land of light—where there is neither "that" nor "this," is what constitutes reaching the other shore.
As for "time," it refers to the time when the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara cultivated this Prajñā;
from antiquity to the present, in the interim, there is no time that can be shifted, no dharma that can be spoken, no movement and no stillness, nor does one abide even in non-movement.
Quiescence that transcends both mundane and supramundane phenomena is what is called "profound.
To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty—
this emptiness of the five aggregates is the emptiness of *prajñā*, which is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and is characterized by cessation.
Once one has departed from mind, intellect, and consciousness, it is seen that there is only mind; this is what is meant by "only through mind-only does one begin to dwell in the ancient abode.
When one no longer dwells in the ancient abode, great function manifests before one, unrestricted by rules.
It delivers one from all suffering and calamity.
All suffering does not transcend the three types of suffering; since the three types of suffering are fundamentally non-existent, the absence of suffering is quiescence (*nirvāṇa*).
Quiescence is the delusion regarding this single mind, whereby manifold sufferings arise. To awaken to this single mind is simply to realize the pure Buddha.
This is the supernormal power of sporting in the buddha-fields.
Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
In the Sanskrit language, Śāri means "Sparrow" (*śārikā*); because his mother was named thus, he is called Śāriputra, the "Son of the Sparrow.

Among those of the Two Vehicles who possess the wisdom of emptiness, he is ranked as the foremost. Now, as his capacity for the profound Prajñāpāramitā is about to ripen, he is summoned and addressed.
That they are not different means that form and emptiness are of one essence, which is the fundamental limit (*koṭi*) where time does not differ.
This is what is meant by "seeing blue and yellow apart from the two eyes" and "discerning right and wrong within emptiness.
That which is "form itself is emptiness" does not mean analyzing phenomena to clarify emptiness, nor does it mean merging them so they cannot be distinguished.

When emptiness and form are clearly manifest and evident, this is the manifestation of signs within the timelessness of non-existence, the preaching of the Dharma within the wordless, and the teaching through no gate.
The gate of non-duality, which exists uniquely and without distinction amidst arising and ceasing—is this not the profound *prajñā*?
As for "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness," these are examples of the four aggregates of mental factors (*citta-dharma*), analogous to the preceding.
Śāriputra, all dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness: they are neither born nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.
That the dharmas—namely the aforementioned five aggregates and so forth—have the characteristic of emptiness is precisely the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Within the essence of this true reality, there is no birth or extinction, no defilement or purity, and no increase or decrease. In this way, one brings the five aggregates back to their true reality.
Regarding what is called "neither arising nor ceasing," it is simply because within this very reality-mark (*dharmatā*), there is no origination or cessation. As the Sūtra says:
"It arises in this very place and perishes in that very place. This is not only so at the level of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*);
even throughout the seventy-nine years from when the World-Honored One descended from Tuṣita Heaven to the royal palace, entered the womb, was born, and finally attained *nirvāṇa*, it remains thus.
It is also as the ancient masters have said: "Without leaving Tuṣita, he was already born in the royal palace;

without emerging from the womb, his work of saving sentient beings was already complete. Truly, these words are so! Within this single limit, the most quiescent state, there is no room for mind or consciousness.
Since even mind and consciousness do not exist, how could there be defilement or purity, increase or decrease?
Thus it is said. Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
As for the statement that "in emptiness there is no form," etc., it is called "non-existent" because not even the slightest dharma can be accommodated within a single kṣaṇa.
This very moment is the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata;
furthermore, within this single instant of teaching the Dharma and delivering sentient beings, it is the differentiated wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).
Since the differentiated wisdom and the fundamental wisdom are established simultaneously, one does not speak of their emptiness, but merely says they are "non-existent."
"No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma; no realm of the eye, and so forth, up to no realm of consciousness.

Regarding the statement that there is "no eye, ear, nose, tongue, etc.," this means that the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) do not appear as entities external to [the nature of reality]. As the Patriarch said:
The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects; its essence reveals the true and eternal, unbound by words and letters.
Simply by being free from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness. The Buddhas and patriarchs breathe from a single nostril; this sutra points directly to the source of the mind.
Because sentient beings are unable to accept and take it up immediately, it employs the three contemplations to lead them to that realization.

The Venerable Nāgārjuna stated: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions—I declare them to be empty; they are also designated as provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
To have these four lines emerge from a single utterance, perfectly accords with and realizes the wondrousness of Prajñā—how could there be anything superior to this?
Because sentient beings are deluded regarding this, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*); because the sages awaken to this, it is called [wisdom].
It transcends number and measure. Why? It is because the three contemplations return to the one mind; the one mind returns to a single kṣaṇa.
Within that single kṣaṇa, there is simply no discursive thought. Because there is no discursive thought, the kṣaṇa-mind cannot exist as a self-subsisting entity.

Therefore, it is said to transcend number and measure. Beyond number and measure, from within the pure mind, the essence and function of the Dharmadhātu emerge as the dependent origination of phenomena.
Are not these dharmas precisely the myriad subtle functions within the Tathāgatagarbha?
There is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance, and so on, up to neither old age and death nor the exhaustion of old age and death.
This is not a system of dependent origination consisting of the twelve links of existence; rather, it is the simultaneous arising of cause and effect across the three periods of time.
Not only do the followers of the Two Vehicles and even Bodhisattvas fail to fully exhaust its principle, but only the Buddha possesses the complete and simultaneous causes and conditions;
therefore, it is called the subtle and wondrous great function. The Treatise says: "In one link, all twelve links are contained; in each and every link, they are all present."
The twelve links comprise one hundred and forty-four links; each link possesses both the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.
Why is this? When a Pratyekabuddha awakens to these, they constitute the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

When an ordinary person possesses them, they become eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), resulting in immeasurable birth and death. When a sage possesses them, they become eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇīs*.
Thus, there are immeasurable Dharma-gates. Why is this? The gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all ultimately return to the single limit of one kṣaṇa.

Within this single kṣaṇa-limit, not even a single dharma can find accommodation; yet the minds of all sages and ordinary beings are entirely contained within this limit, and it is able to pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
The body of universal wisdom manifests everywhere, appearing nowhere it does not reach.
There is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path.
There is no Four Noble Truths of the Hīnayāna, because it directly points out that the Śrāvaka is itself Nirvāṇa. Why is this?

Because suffering is itself Nirvāṇa, and the origin is itself all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*). However, one must understand the significance of these two instances of the word "itself" (*eva*).
Without expending even a hair’s breadth of effort, one suddenly accords with the principle of Prajñā. Why is this? Because there are no three periods of time.
Since there are no three periods of time, there is no self, person, sentient being, or life-span. One realizes it without cultivation;

therefore, sentient beings are themselves Buddhas, for sentient beings and Buddhas are fundamentally of one and the same aspect. As the Sūtra says: "This Dharma abides in the station of Dharma within the world."
If the marks are eternally abiding, why must they transform?
There is neither ignorance nor attainment.
Within this sutra, there is no dharma that abides; even the wisdom that can realize it and the nirvana realized by that wisdom are merely provisional expressions.
Because there are no real dharmas, the Sūtra states that wisdom and ignorance are both termed *prajñā*, and that purity and impurity, self and other, have no difference in their realm.

However, regarding the three aggregates (*skandhas*), seven elements (*dhātus*), and twelve bases (*āyatanas*) spoken of by the World-Honored One—which are the objects of cultivation and realization for Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas—one must not simply claim they do not exist. This is precisely what the World-Honored One meant when he spoke of "all."

This signifies that the ultimate reality is firm and unshakable. Those today who aspire to advance on the Path must not establish their practice apart from the phenomena of everyday life (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).
If one establishes practice apart from these phenomena, there will inevitably be error and deviation; it will not be ultimate.
Therefore, within the section on the "Correct Teaching," the single word "No" (*wu*) is spoken precisely to indicate that no words are established upon the phenomena of everyday life.
The principle of taking the mind as the object of the written word is precisely what is called the Prajñā of the Supreme Vehicle of the Dharma’s “special transmission outside the teachings.
As it has been said of old: "If one gazes at it through the lens of phenomenal appearances, one merely conjectures upon the faculty of the intellect;
one will only grope about and fail to grasp it."
Because there is nothing to be attained.
That is to say, the primordial wisdom is without dependence and without abiding; because the fundamental dharma is inconceivable, it is said that "there is no attainment."
"Bodhisattvas rely on the perfection of wisdom.
"Bodhisattva" refers to the person who practices; "rely on" means to depend upon or to lean against, specifically leaning upon this momentary primordial limit (*kṣaṇa-mūla-koṭi*).
When the mind is without hindrance, because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; one is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, reaching ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
This is the realization attained by those who enter the Samādhi of the Momentary Limit and contemplate the sentient beings of the six realms and the worthy and holy ones of the three vehicles.
The nirvāṇa realized through wisdom is collectively termed nothing but inverted dreams and delusions;
if one can thus comprehend and grasp this without losing the essential purport of this sutra, only then is it called the Great Ultimate within the ocean of great quiescence.
Hereafter, this sutra is praised to reveal the reality of prajñā.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This citation is intended to lead those capable of realization to verify that this sutra is not false, so that those who hear it may give rise to true faith. Thus it is obtained.
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is precisely the Unsurpassed, Perfect, and Equal Enlightenment.
World-Honored One, because at the moment of entering the limit of the kṣaṇa (the ultimate instant), there is not a single dharma that can be added above it, it is called "unsurpassed.
Because within the fundamental limit all Buddhas and sentient beings are equal and non-dual, it is called "perfectly equal and perfect enlightenment," which is to say, the fundamental [nature].

To be deluded regarding this awakening is called non-awakening; to awaken to this awakening is called initial awakening. Since this awakening is fundamentally devoid of delusion and enlightenment, it is termed "original awakening.
These three types of awakening are merely provisional designations; they have no substantial reality and are spoken of only as a skillful means to point toward perfect awakening.
Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra,
the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra.
The secret of Prajñā is non-action, non-ceasing, non-effort, non-extinction, neither non-existence nor wisdom.

Because light is fundamentally of one characteristic, one knows that this sutra is a great mantra (*mahā-mantra*) beyond the fathom of the mind, for it is the inconceivable supernatural transformations employed by all Buddhas;
it is a great luminous mantra (*mahā-vidyā-mantra*), for through the wisdom of non-discrimination, it employs the equality of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) to awaken sentient beings;
it is an unsurpassed mantra (*anuttara-mantra*), for if sentient beings of great resolve awaken to this Dharma...
Because the initial mind of the ten stages is equal and no different from the fruit-stage of all Buddhas, it is called the "Unequaled Mantra";
for it is the unsurpassed Dharma realized by the Buddha, which nothing else can surpass.
Because it is able to eliminate all suffering and is true and not false, the *Prajñāpāramitā* mantra is spoken.
The mantra is as follows: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*. This sutra and its mantra interweave the exoteric and the esoteric;
the wise who directly awaken to the samādhi within every dust-mote will then accord with this.

This is the marrow of the sutras. Why? Because the sages and ordinary beings alike perceive that all things—the vast array of the great earth, humans, animals, and so forth—are none other than the manifestation of Prajñā.
The phrases *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā* emerge from and dissolve into this sutra.
Taking profound Prajñā as its essential framework, the non-difference between form and emptiness as its central tenet, and the empty nature of all phenomena as its essence, it upholds the word "No."
When one acts as a non-user, not even a speck of dust can be established; by relying on the seed-syllable "non-existence" (*wu*), one is able to contain the myriad existents.

That which is without form, without sensation, and so forth, up to without wisdom and without attainment—is this not the profound *prajñā* beyond words and transcending thought, the teaching outside [the scriptures]?
As for the various dharmas such as form, sensation, and emptiness, they were first bestowed upon the bhikṣus...
Why is it that even the fruit of Buddhahood can be contained within the "letterless"? It is because all phenomena are the union of emptiness with emptiness;
thus, they attain unimpeded containment. Nowadays, among those who wish to see emptiness, six or seven out of ten fall into this error.

This is because they fail to realize that this Prajñā is ultimately detached from words and letters, and that it is through awakening beyond both emptiness and form that one understands what is and is not contained. Therefore, [this is] the first point.
All inversions are themselves nirvāṇa.
*The Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom* (End). The Commentary states:
What has been explained above regarding the "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) is the wondrous function of the primordial limit (*koṭi*). Why is this so?
Because the fundamental limit (*koṭi*) has no coming or going, it is able to encompass the three periods of time;
because it abides not for even a single moment, it is without inherent nature, yet possesses great capacity, great function, and great mastery.

Since these two dharmas are fundamentally non-different, if one takes this essential limit as the substance for teaching and transforming sentient beings, one may establish a single character as the substance and the three categories and seven elements as the function. If one takes this...
In terms of ultimate application, one establishes a single word as the function and the three categories and seven elements as the essence;
for neither Buddhas nor patriarchs ever depart from the moment of a single instant (*kṣaṇa*). Suppose there is a person who enters a forest hermitage (*araṇya*);

when they take their first step and tread upon a single brick, hundreds of bricks have already been traversed. If one were to walk by stages through these hundred bricks, it would simply be returning to the origin.
Just as the initial bricks laid down do not move, so too is the essence and function of this Prajñā.

In the age of the Final Dharma, there are those who cling to this mind as existing, those who cling to it as empty, those who cling to it as permanent, those who cling to it as impermanent, those who cling to it as knowing, and those who cling to it as not knowing; yet these—permanence and impermanence, knowing and not knowing—are all fused [within it].

Those who hold to "pervasion," those who hold to "total non-existence," those who hold that there is no form within the mind, those who hold that there is no mind within form, those who hold that there is form within the mind, those who hold that there is mind within form, those who hold to "pervasiveness" and "non-pervasiveness," those who hold to "analogy," and those who hold to "dharmas"—such attachments as these cannot be enumerated individually;
they are all merely conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). As it is said:
All that has been discussed here ultimately converges within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). It is neither gathered nor dispersed, neither coming nor going, without abiding and without dependence.
Why is this? Because its nature is equal, its time is equal, its practice is equal, its essence and function are equal, and its cause and effect are equal.
This mind is equal to the Buddha, equal to sentient beings, and equal to the *dharmadhātu*. Furthermore, this mind is not identical to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Nor is there anything called "one mind" apart from the four propositions, nor "three periods of time" apart from one mind.
To raise a single hair-tip and yet cause it to pervade the entire universe—only those who understand in this way accord with the essential principle of the Prajñāpāramitā heart.
The World-Honored One, the General of the Non-Dual, has pointed out the Heart Sutra of No-Syllables to guide those who are deluded.
Nowadays, people take this "no-syllable" as a basis to debate it against "syllables," thereby giving rise to words of both establishment and slander. How so?
They establish a nature that is not "existence," establishing a nature that is not "non-existence," and establishing a nature that is neither existence nor non-existence.
How is it that by establishing a nature where there is neither existence nor non-existence, one falls into the verbal expression of eternalism by asserting existence where there is none,
the verbal expression of nihilism by asserting non-existence where there is none, the verbal expression of the "both" view by asserting both existence and non-existence as identical,
and the verbal expression of the "neither" view by asserting something apart from both existence and non-existence? This is [the question].

Regarding the establishment of names and the refutation of dharmas—apart from the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, the practices of all other teachings cannot avoid falling into the ranks of externalists and māras because they grasp at and cling to them.
Within the sphere of activity of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, things can be gathered together and split apart;
whatever is picked up by hand is spontaneously free. Although there are various distinctions, within the One...
Because the dharmas at the limit of a single instant are equal and non-dual in accordance with their true nature, they are called "sovereign.
Now, the essence of Prajñā is numinous clarity, neither one nor many; yet when people raise it into function, there are distinctions.
There is no lack of great utility here: for the wise, all is one in function; for those of insight, one is all. Thus, the one and the many are identical.
The various teachings of the Half- and Full-Turning [Wheels] do not transcend the great function of the "Wordless" (*amala*), from which the seven treasures and eight jewels leak forth.
This means that when one seizes and displays it directly before one’s face, its essence is manifest and without partiality; it is not something that can be discussed by ordinary people.

Even regarding those in the netherworld, humans and animals, horizontal and vertical, bending and stretching, speaking and remaining silent, in meditative stillness, or in the perception of what is to the left and right—first realize this within it.
Because a single eye behind the face can eliminate all suffering, and because it is true and not false, the mantra of the Prajñāpāramitā is spoken.
The sharpness of Prajñā is difficult to depict; how could one find a place to dwell within the flames of the Vajra?
Failing to realize the intimate state of profound stillness, one turns the light back for a single illumination that pierces through a thousand layers.
*The Decisive Resolution on the Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* (End).
Postscript by the two commentaries of Master Liang of Beichan.
Among those of us who study, what is obtained through formal transmission is shallow, while what is obtained through the celestial mechanism (tianji) is deep;

this is true even for worldly learning, let alone the Buddha-dharma. Master Lianggong, possessing a nature of profound substance and accumulating a sincere yearning, strove tirelessly to present his points of awakening to the world.
Indeed, from the very beginning, he had already picked up these truths upon his straw sandals as he traversed thousands of mountains and ten thousand rivers.

In the latter part of the night, upon my meditation cushion, I take up this matter; it is not like those worldly masters who consume the spittle and snot of others, seeking a livelihood from the "Yellow Book" of smoke and ashes.
Last year, the *Ji jue* (Decisions on the Heart Sutra) was circulated in the world;
before long, the *Mi tuo ji jue* (Decisions on Amitābha) also appeared. Indeed, one enters through the gate of wisdom and returns to the Pure Land, tracing the current back to its source.
The source is found through the branches, leading back to the root. Long ago, Mañjuśrī, possessing great wisdom, made a vow to seek rebirth in the Western Land;

Master Liang’s exposition of the original intent of this work accords with that in a hidden way. This must surely be because the Buddhas, moved by compassion for his diligence, have silently provided their support.
Written on the eve of the New Year in the year of Renwu by the disciple Xu Bo.
If a person realizes the mind, there is not an inch of ground in the Great Earth; Prajñā is the mind and the Pure Land is the ground of the mind.
These two sutras are the eternal principle of the mind, and these two commentaries are the guide to the mind.
Therefore, apart from the mind, there is neither Prajñā nor a Pure Land, let alone these two sutras and two commentaries. Within the two commentaries, it is said:
The limits of atoms and the limits of moments refer to the source of the mind before even a single thought has arisen.
To maintain this source of the mind is called practicing profound *prajñā*; to reach this source of the mind is called the practice of rebirth in the Pure Land.
To go there, one must necessarily rely on a guide to know the direction and location; thus, these two sutras cannot do without their two commentaries.
It is just so. I, the old man in meditative concentration, the Chan Master Yuezhou Hu, happened upon this book;
as I read it, I was filled with joy and desired to share it with the assembly. I have therefore ordered it to be carved and printed for circulation.
This is a heart of great compassion, a heart of *prajñā*, and a heart of adornment for the Pure Land. These three hearts are but one heart, arising from that subtle...
Flowing forth from the two limits of every dust-mote and instant, it covers heaven and earth, vast and without bound.
Since this mind is itself without boundary, how could the circulation of this book also have any limit? It is my good fortune to be among the first to read and examine it;
I know not what measure of gratitude and joy I should feel. Thus, I have taken up this worn brush at the end of the scroll to briefly record the date and year.

Thus it is said. On an auspicious day of the third month in the fifth year of the Wucheng era, at the Mahayana Huguo Chan Temple in Jiazu Suzhulin, I, Baimanshan, respectfully offer my salutations. Postscript.
